    Laplace's equation

    See [axl2013, gtr2001].

    Problem. Consider

    \begin{equation} \Delta u=0 \text { in } \Omega \quad \text{or} \quad \Delta u=f \text { in } \Omega. \end{equation}

    Remark

    Usaully, we only consider \(\Omega\) is a bound domain, and the Green formula is valid.

    Example
    1. \(u(x)=\left(x^{1}\right)^{2}-\left(x^{2}\right)^{2}\).
    2. 1, \(x_1,\cdots, x_n,x_{i}^{2}-x_{j}^{2},x_{i}x_{j}(i\neq j), (3x_{i}^{2}-x_{j}^2)x_{j}\). These are called harmnic polynomials.
    3. Real and imaginary part of holomorphic functions.
    Definition

    The fundamental solution in \(\rr^d\) is given by

    \begin{equation} \Gamma(x, y)=\Gamma(|x-y|):= \begin{cases}\frac{1}{2 \pi} \log |x-y| & \text { for } d=2 \\ \frac{1}{d(2-d) \omega_{d}}|x-y|^{2-d} & \text { for } d>2\end{cases} \end{equation}

    Here \(\omega _d \) is the volume of unit ball in \(\rr^d\).

    Theorem

    Assume \(u \in C^{2}(\bar{\Omega}), y\in \Omega\). Then

    \begin{equation} u(y)=\int_{\partial \Omega}\left\{u(x) \frac{\partial \Gamma}{\partial v_{x}}(x, y)-\Gamma(x, y) \frac{\partial u}{\partial v}(x)\right\} d S(x)+\int_{\Omega} \Gamma(x, y) \Delta u(x) \mathrm{d} x \end{equation}

    Theorem

    Assume \(\varphi \in C^{0}(\partial B_R(0))\), then the following Dirichlet problem has unique solution \(u\in C^{2} (B_R(0)) \cap C^{0}(\overline{B}_R(0))\).

    \[ \begin{cases} &\Delta u(x)=0 \quad \text { for } x \in B_R(0),\\ &u(x)=\varphi(x) \quad \text { for } x \in \partial B_R(0) . \end{cases} \]

    The solution can be expressed by

    \[ u(y):= \begin{cases}\frac{R^{2}-|y|^{2}}{d \omega_{d} R} \int_{\partial B_R(0)} \frac{\varphi(x)}{|x-y|^{d}} d S(x) & \text { for } y \in B_R(0) \\ \varphi(y) & \text { for } y \in \partial B_R(0)\end{cases}. \]

    Corollary

    Harmonic function is analytic.

    Theorem (Mean value property)

    For any harmonic function \(u\), we have

    \[ u(x)=\fint_{\partial B(x, r)} u d S=\fint_{B(x, r)} u d y. \]

    Theorem (Weyl lemma)

    If \(u\) is locally integrable on \(\Omega\), and

    \[ \int_{\Omega} u(x) \Delta \varphi(x) \mathrm{d} x=0, \quad \forall \varphi \in C_{0}^{\infty}(\Omega). \]

    Then \(u\) is harmonic, and in particula, \(u\) is smooth.

    Theorem (maximum principal)

    If \(\Delta u\geq 0\) and \(u\) attains maximum at interior point, then \(u\) is constant.

    Theorem (Singularity removable [jost2013])

    If \(u\) is harmonic outside a point in domain with dimension \(\geq 2\), and \(u\) is bounded, then \(u\) is harmonic.

    We know from this that Laplace's equation does not always have a solution.

    Theorem (Liouville theorem)

    Assume \(u: \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) is bounded harmonic function, then \(u\) is constant.

    Theorem ([jost2013])

    Let \(u: \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be a nonnegative harmonic function, then \(u\) is constant.

    Theorem (Harnack inequality)

    Assume \(u\) is a nonnegative harmonic function on \(\Omega \), then

    \[ \sup _{\Omega^{\prime}} u \leq c \inf _{\Omega^{\prime}} u . \]

    where \(c=c\left(d, \Omega, \Omega^{\prime}\right),\Omega^{\prime} \subset \subset \Omega\).

    Theorem (monotone convergence)

    Suppose \(\{u_n\}\) is a sequence of monotone increasing harmnic functions, and \(\exists y\in \Omega\) s.t. \(\{u_n(y)\}\) is bounded. Then \(\{u_n\}\) locally converges to a harmonic function.

    From mean value property, we have

    Theorem

    If a sequence of harmonic functions uniformly converge to a function, then the limit function is also harmonic.

    According to gradient estimates [gtr2001]:

    Theorem (Normal family)

    Any bouded harmonic functions sequence has subsequence uniformly converging in a compact domain.

    Theorem

    Suppose \(u\) is harmonic on unit ball, denote

    \[ H(r)=\fint_{\partial B(x, r)} u^2 d S, \quad D(r)=r^2 \fint_{B(x, r)} |\nabla u|^2 d y. \]

    Then \(H(r),D(r), \frac{D(r)}{H(r)}\) are monotone increasing.
